summary.text: At \(n=473165\), the Sierpiński number \(K=5292270077783\) lies strictly between the endpoints \(5292270077779\) and \(5292270077807\). Its Sierpiński property follows from a covering of all exponent residues modulo \(48\): according to the residue of \(m\), one of \(3,5,7,17,97,257,673\) is a proper divisor of \(K2^m+1\), so this intermediate number disproves consecutiveness.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=9{,}454{,}129+11{,}184{,}810n.
\]
Recall that a Sierpiński number is an odd integer \(k>1\) such that
\[
k2^m+1
\]
is composite for every positive integer \(m\). We will disprove the conjecture by giving one index \(n\) for which there is another Sierpiński number strictly between \(a(n)\) and \(a(n)+28\).

Set
\[
K=5{,}292{,}270{,}077{,}783.
\]
We first prove that \(K\) is a Sierpiński number. Clearly \(K\) is odd and \(K>1\). It remains to show that \(K2^m+1\) is composite for every positive integer \(m\).

We use a covering of all exponents by congruence classes modulo \(48\). The elementary periodicity principle needed below is the following: if
\[
2^g\equiv 1\pmod p
\]
and \(m\equiv s\pmod g\), then
\[
2^m\equiv 2^s\pmod p.
\]
Indeed, writing \(m=qg+s\), one has
\[
2^m=(2^g)^q2^s\equiv 2^s\pmod p.
\]

The relevant modular computations are summarized in this table:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c}
p&g&s&K\bmod p&2^g\bmod p&2^s\bmod p\\ \hline
3&2&0&2&1&1\\
5&4&3&3&1&3\\
7&3&1&3&1&2\\
17&8&1&8&1&2\\
257&16&5&8&1&32\\
97&48&29&94&1&65\\
673&48&45&665&1&589
\end{array}
\]
In every row, the last two relevant residues satisfy
\[
(K\bmod p)(2^s\bmod p)+1\equiv0\pmod p.
\]
More explicitly, these checks are
\[
2\cdot1+1=3,
\qquad 3\cdot3+1=10,
\qquad 3\cdot2+1=7,
\]
\[
8\cdot2+1=17,
\qquad 8\cdot32+1=257,
\]
\[
94\cdot65+1=6111=97\cdot63,
\]
and
\[
665\cdot589+1=391686=673\cdot582.
\]
Thus, whenever the exponent \(m\) has the residue specified in a row, the corresponding \(p\) divides \(K2^m+1\).

For completeness, all of the period and residue entries in the table follow from direct integer arithmetic. For the small periods,
\[
2^2=4\equiv1\pmod3,
\quad 2^4=16\equiv1\pmod5,
\quad 2^3=8\equiv1\pmod7,
\]
\[
2^8=256\equiv1\pmod{17},
\quad 2^{16}=65536=257\cdot255+1.
\]
For the two periods of length \(48\),
\[
2^{48}=281{,}474{,}976{,}710{,}656
       =97\cdot2{,}901{,}803{,}883{,}615+1
\]
and
\[
2^{48}=673\cdot418{,}239{,}192{,}735+1.
\]
The two less immediate power residues are
\[
2^{29}=536{,}870{,}912=97\cdot5{,}534{,}751+65
\]
and
\[
2^{45}=35{,}184{,}372{,}088{,}832
      =673\cdot52{,}279{,}899{,}091+589.
\]
The residues of \(K\) can likewise be read from
\[
\begin{aligned}
K&=3\cdot1{,}764{,}090{,}025{,}927+2,\\
K&=5\cdot1{,}058{,}454{,}015{,}556+3,\\
K&=7\cdot756{,}038{,}582{,}540+3,\\
K&=17\cdot311{,}310{,}004{,}575+8,\\
K&=257\cdot20{,}592{,}490{,}575+8,\\
K&=97\cdot54{,}559{,}485{,}337+94,\\
K&=673\cdot7{,}863{,}699{,}966+665.
\end{aligned}
\]

We now explain why these rows cover every exponent. Let \(r\) be the residue of \(m\) modulo \(48\), so \(0\le r<48\).

1. If \(r\) is even, then \(m\equiv0\pmod2\). The first row applies, so
\[
3\mid K2^m+1.
\]

2. If \(r\equiv3\pmod4\), namely if
\[
r\in\{3,7,11,15,19,23,27,31,35,39,43,47\},
\]
then \(m\equiv3\pmod4\). The second row applies, so
\[
5\mid K2^m+1.
\]

The only residues not yet treated are the odd residues congruent to \(1\pmod4\). They split as follows.

3. If
\[
r\in\{1,13,25,37\},
\]
then \(m\equiv1\pmod3\), so the row for \(p=7\) gives
\[
7\mid K2^m+1.
\]

4. If
\[
r\in\{9,17,33,41\},
\]
then \(m\equiv1\pmod8\), so the row for \(p=17\) gives
\[
17\mid K2^m+1.
\]

5. If
\[
r\in\{5,21\},
\]
then \(m\equiv5\pmod{16}\), so the row for \(p=257\) gives
\[
257\mid K2^m+1.
\]

6. If \(r=29\), then \(m\equiv29\pmod{48}\), and the row for \(p=97\) gives
\[
97\mid K2^m+1.
\]

7. Finally, if \(r=45\), then \(m\equiv45\pmod{48}\), and the row for \(p=673\) gives
\[
673\mid K2^m+1.
\]

These cases are exhaustive: the even residues account for all 24 even classes modulo \(48\); the second case accounts for the 12 odd classes congruent to \(3\pmod4\); and the sets in cases 3–7 are precisely the remaining 12 classes
\[
1,5,9,13,17,21,25,29,33,37,41,45.
\]
Consequently, for every positive integer \(m\), at least one of
\[
3,5,7,17,257,97,673
\]
divides \(K2^m+1\).

Each of these divisors is greater than \(1\). It is also strictly smaller than \(K2^m+1\), since every one is at most \(673\), whereas
\[
K2^m+1\ge K+1>673.
\]
Therefore \(K2^m+1\) has a proper nontrivial divisor and is composite. This holds for every positive \(m\), so, together with the facts that \(K\) is odd and greater than \(1\), it proves that \(K\) is a Sierpiński number.

Now take
\[
n=473{,}165.
\]
A direct calculation gives
\[
11{,}184{,}810\cdot473{,}165=5{,}292{,}260{,}623{,}650,
\]
so
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(473{,}165)
&=9{,}454{,}129+5{,}292{,}260{,}623{,}650\\
&=5{,}292{,}270{,}077{,}779.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence
\[
a(473{,}165)+28=5{,}292{,}270{,}077{,}807.
\]
Our Sierpiński number \(K\) satisfies
\[
K=5{,}292{,}270{,}077{,}783
  =a(473{,}165)+4.
\]
In particular,
\[
a(473{,}165)<K<a(473{,}165)+28.
\]
Thus there is a Sierpiński number strictly between \(a(473{,}165)\) and \(a(473{,}165)+28\). Those two numbers therefore cannot be consecutive Sierpiński numbers. This single index \(n=473{,}165\) disproves the assertion that \(a(n)\) and \(a(n)+28\) are consecutive Sierpiński numbers for every \(n\ge0\).
